one_line: LUSCA trained the tokenizer for SEPIA-1, its planned code-reading model: a 32,768-entry byte-level BPE built for smart-contract and protocol code, measured on held-out files against the GPT tokenizers, and running in the browser on lusca.ink/sepia. The SEPIA-1 model itself is not trained yet.
status_rules: Milestone M1 (tokenizer) is done: trained, evaluated, shipped in the app. SEPIA-1, the model, is not trained yet. Say so whenever the tokenizer is shown.
The Hugging Face repo LUSCAINK/SEPIA-1-tokenizer is prepared but NOT uploaded. Only mention Hugging Face after the owner has run the upload.
Everything is local until the owner pushes and deploys. Do not say it is live on lusca.ink before the deploy.

facts.value: 4.6% fewer than o200k_base, 5.1% fewer than cl100k_base, 43.0% fewer than GPT-2 r50k_base (1,464,683 vs 1,535,365 / 1,543,300 / 2,569,197 tokens on 6.19 MB, 171,376 lines)

facts.value: Solidity 4.44 vs 4.27 · Rust/Anchor 4.44 vs 4.21 · Move 4.20 vs 4.09 · Cairo 3.83 vs 3.76 · Go 3.87 vs 3.67 · Vyper 4.34 vs 3.93 (15 files) · TypeScript 4.30 vs 3.91 (16 files) · Python 4.61 vs 4.24 (15 files) · C/C++ 3.78 vs 3.80 (9 files; cl100k 3.81 is best)

facts.value: English crypto web text 3.79 bytes/token vs o200k 4.26 and cl100k 4.15 (r50k 3.80); Markdown docs/EIPs 3.54 vs o200k 3.67; C/C++ 3.78 vs cl100k 3.81. The 32k vocabulary is 3-6x smaller than cl100k/o200k, which keeps the SEPIA-1 embedding table small for volunteer GPUs.

facts.fact: Why the parity holds in every browser
facts.value: The TypeScript encoder replaces the regex classes \p{L} and \p{N} with the exact code-point sets the Python tokenizer uses (131,756 letter and 1,791 number code points, measured over all of Unicode). With the engine's own classes, Node 24 (Unicode 16) disagreed with Python on 548 of the 5,518 test strings.

facts.value: Training twice gives a byte-identical tokenizer.json (sha256 4b2ec96ed69a7c9fe7a7c01bd01e4d4c95f527384d6ee3862e43e850ed54d04f); training took 24.6 s on the local CPU

209.22 MB sample, 26,411 documents. 61.8% from the protocol code index (49.5% source code, 11.8% Markdown docs and EIPs, 0.5% Anchor IDL JSON): all 110 allowlisted repositories, 18,239 files, each with its license. 38.2% (80.0 MB, 10,595 pages) crypto web text sampled with a fixed seed from the LUSCA corpus.

1,052 documents set aside by hash before training and never trained on: 8% of code files per language (up to 1.5 MB each) plus 202 English web pages. Code is held out by file, so other files of the same repositories are in training.
Not used: the public chain API exposes source paths and sizes, not source text

A line break plus the next line's indentation is one token; multi-character operators (=> -> :: == != <= >= && || << >> += -= ** // /* */ ..= /// #[) are never split; identifiers and dotted chains like msg.sender are units BPE can learn; numbers are one digit per token; hex literals over 8 digits are cut into 0x plus 4-digit groups so addresses and hashes do not use up the vocabulary.

Pan across the six stat tiles: 32,768 vocabulary; 4.22 bytes/token on held-out code (o200k 4.03, cl100k 4.01); -4.6% tokens vs o200k; -43.0% vs GPT-2 r50k; 100% exact round trip; 0 diff browser vs Python.

On the default Solmate ERC4626 example, hover a few chips: 'msg.sender' is one token, '↵····' (newline plus indentation) is one token, ' !=' and ' =>' stay whole. The inspector shows the id and byte count.
Point at 'HELD OUT · NOT IN TRAINING' and the repo@commit · path · line link and license under the editor.
Click o200k, then cl100k in the switch above the chips; then back to SEPIA-1. Counts: 201 / 205 / 207.
Click OpenBook v2 (Anchor, Rust): 290 vs 309 vs 305. Click OpenZeppelin Cairo: 280 vs 323 vs 324. DeepBook Move is 264 vs 257: SEPIA-1 uses more on that excerpt; it can be shown, it is honest.
Click 'color · tokens' to switch to 'color · length': longer tokens glow brighter orange.
Click 'your code', paste a contract (any Solidity file). The GPT encodings load on first edit (about 1.5 MB); counts update as you type. Nothing is sent to the server.

Scroll to 'held-out evaluation'. Switch bytes / token -> tokens / 1,000 lines -> lines / 2,048 window (Solidity 225 vs o200k 216, Rust 258 vs 245). The best cell in each row is highlighted, including the rows SEPIA-1 loses (C/C++, Markdown, web text).
Show the six rule cards: indentation, operators, identifiers, digits, hex (0x dAC1 7F95 ...), bytes.
Footer: 'download tokenizer.json', 'model card', 'eval table', 'manifest · sha256' open the served files.
At phone width the table shows SEPIA-1 vs o200k for every language; chips wrap only between tokens.

avoid: crawl, crawler, crawling (say: agents read, the corpus, the code index)
INK points (say: credits); do not connect the tokenizer to $INK
'SEPIA-1 is trained', 'SEPIA-1 is live', 'our model reads code' (only the tokenizer is done; the model is not trained yet)
'beats GPT-4o / OpenAI / ChatGPT' (this compares tokenizer encodings, o200k_base and cl100k_base, not models)
'best tokenizer for all code' or 'wins every language' (C/C++ is a near tie that cl100k wins; prose and Markdown are worse)
a single example's percentage as the headline (for example '-13% on Cairo'); use the held-out totals: -4.6% vs o200k, -5.1% vs cl100k
'trained on verified on-chain contracts' (on-chain sources were not used for this tokenizer)
'available on Hugging Face' before the owner uploads it
slogans and hype: revolutionary, game-changing, first ever, unmatched, next-gen
